==Problem==
What is the units digit of <math>2022^{2023} + 2023^{2022}</math>?

<math>\text{(A)}\ 7 \qquad \text{(B)}\ 1 \qquad \text{(C)}\ 9 \qquad \text{(D)}\ 5 \qquad \text{(E)}\ 3</math>

==Solution 1==
<math>2022^{2023} + 2023^{2022} \equiv 2^3 + 3^2 \equiv 17 \equiv 7</math> (mod 10). <math>\boxed{\text{A}}</math>
~andliu766

The method omits many steps, and it is important to note that we do not have <math> a\equiv b\pmod{m}\Rightarrow c^{a}\equiv c^{b}\pmod{m} </math>. For example, <math> 5\equiv 2\pmod{3} </math>, but <math> 2^{5}\equiv2\not\equiv1\equiv2^{2}\pmod{3} </math>.

==Solution 2==
When looking at the units digit patterns of the powers of <math>2</math>, we see that 

<math>2^1=</math>,  units digit <math>2</math>

<math>2^2=</math>,  units digit <math>4</math>

<math>2^3=</math>,  units digit <math>8</math>

<math>2^4=</math>,  units digit <math>6</math>

<math>2^5=</math>,  units digit <math>2</math>

And the pattern repeats. This pattern will apply for the powers of <math>2022</math> as well, since the units digit of <math>2022</math> is <math>2</math>. We can find the pattern for the powers of <math>3</math> too. The pattern follows with units digits, <math>3</math>, <math>9</math>, <math>7</math>, <math>1</math>, <math>3</math>, <math>9</math>, ...
Similarly, the units digit of <math>2023</math> will follow the same pattern as the powers of <math>3</math>. 

Both of these powers cycle in groups of <math>4</math>. When diving <math>2023</math> by <math>4</math>, we get <math>505</math> remainder <math>3</math>, meaning <math>505</math> complete cycles; or the power being a multiple of <math>4</math>,  <math>505</math> times, and <math>3</math> extra. So the units digit of <math>2022^{2023}</math> is <math>8</math>. 
<math>2022</math> divided by <math>4</math> is <math>505</math> reminder <math>2</math>, which means <math>505</math> complete cycles, or the power being a multiple of <math>4</math>,  <math>505</math> times, and <math>2</math> extra. So the units digit of <math>2023^{2022}</math> is <math>9</math>.

We only need to find the units digit in the end, so we just add those <math>2</math> already found units digits, to get a new units digit of <math>7</math>. Therefore the answer is <math>\boxed{\text{(A) 7}}</math>

~mk00


==Solution 3 (Digit Cycles)==
Note that the units digit will be the same regardless of the tens, hundreds, and thousands digits, so we can simplify this problem to finding the last digit of <math>2^{2023} + 3^{2022}</math>. We can find the units digit of <math>2^{2023}</math>, by listing the units digits of the first few powers of two, and trying to find a pattern. 

<math>2^1=2</math>

<math>2^2=4</math>

<math>2^3=8</math>

<math>2^4=6+10</math>

<math>2^5=2+30</math>

<math>2^6=4+60</math>

As we can see the units digits of powers of two repeat after every four iterations. Now we know the units digit of <math>2^{2020}</math> is <math>6</math> and the units digit of <math>2^{2023} \Rightarrow 2^3\cdot 2^{2020} \Rightarrow 6\cdot 8 \Rightarrow 8</math>. Similarly we can find the last digits of powers of three repeat after every four, so the units digit of <math>3^{2022}</math> is <math>1\cdot 3^2 = 9</math>. Adding these together, the ones digit is the same as the ones digit of <math>9+8</math> which is <math>7</math>. <math>\boxed{\text{(A) 7}}</math>

~vsinghminhas

== Solution 4 (Bashy) ==

<math>2022^{2023}\equiv 2^{2023}=128^{289}\equiv 8^{289}=2^{289\times3}=131072^{51}\equiv 2^{51}=131072^3\equiv 2^3=8</math> <math>(\text{mod}</math>  <math>10)</math>
<math>2023^{2022}\equiv 3^{2022}=9^{1011}\equiv (-1)^{1011}=-1\equiv 9</math> <math>(\text{mod}</math>  <math>10)</math>

<math>8+9=17\equiv 7</math> <math>(\text{mod}</math>  <math>10)</math>
